info.description:
# Getting Started

The Spiffy API allows you to programmatically manage customers, orders, subscriptions, and more.

## Authentication

The Spiffy API supports two authentication methods. Which one you use depends on the type of integration you're building.

| | API Key | OAuth 2.0 |
|---|---|---|
| **For** | Private integrations | Third-party integrations |
| **Access scope** | Your account only | Any merchant who authorizes your app |
| **Setup** | Create a key in the dashboard | Register OAuth client on Developer Platform |

### API Key

API key authentication is the simplest way to access the Spiffy API. It's intended for private integrations — internal tools and scripts that connect to your own Spiffy account.

Create and manage keys in your Spiffy dashboard under **Settings → API**. An account can hold multiple named keys — for example, one per integration — so you can tell at a glance what each key is used for and revoke one without affecting the others.

Pass a key as a Bearer token in the `Authorization` header on every request:

```
Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY
```

**Security:**
- Treat every key like a password. Do not commit it to version control or expose it in client-side code.
- To rotate a key without downtime, create a new key, cut your integration over to it, then delete the old key.
- If a key is compromised, regenerate it from Settings → API. That invalidates only that key's old secret immediately and issues a new one in its place — other keys on the account are unaffected.

### OAuth 2.0

OAuth 2.0 is required for third-party integrations — apps that connect to other merchants' Spiffy accounts on their behalf.

**Step 1 — Redirect the merchant to authorize:**

```
https://app.spiffy.co/oauth/authorize
  ?client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID
  &redirect_uri=YOUR_REDIRECT_URI
  &response_type=code
  &scope=REQUESTED_SCOPES
  &state=RANDOM_STATE_VALUE
```

The `state` parameter should be a random, unguessable value to prevent CSRF attacks.

**Step 2 — Exchange the authorization code for tokens:**

```
POST https://api.spiffy.co/oauth/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code
&code=AUTHORIZATION_CODE
&client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID
&client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET
&redirect_uri=YOUR_REDIRECT_URI
```

Response:
```json
{
  "access_token": "...",
  "refresh_token": "...",
  "token_type": "bearer",
  "expires_in": 3600
}
```

**Step 3 — Use the access token:**

```
Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN
```

**Step 4 — Refresh when expired:**

Access tokens expire after 1 hour. Refresh tokens are valid for 1 month and are single-use — each refresh issues a new pair.

```
POST https://api.spiffy.co/oauth/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=refresh_token
&refresh_token=REFRESH_TOKEN
&client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID
&client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET
```

**Available scopes:** account, users, customers, checkouts, subscriptions, subscription_metered_billing, integrations, orders, payments, paymentplans, webhooks

**Token security:**
- Store tokens securely — treat them like passwords
- Never expose tokens in client-side code, URLs, or logs
- Merchants can revoke access at any time; handle 401 responses gracefully

## Rate Limiting

API requests are subject to two types of rate limiting:

### Per-Minute Rate Limit

- **100 requests per 60-second window** (fixed window)
- Applies to account API key requests only. Approved third-party developer applications are metered separately and are subject to neither the per-minute limit nor the monthly quota.
- Response headers on every request:
  - `X-RateLimit-Limit`: Maximum requests allowed (100)
  - `X-RateLimit-Remaining`: Requests remaining in current window
  - `X-RateLimit-Reset`: Unix timestamp when the window resets

### Monthly Request Quota

Monthly limits are based on your Spiffy subscription plan:

| Plan | Monthly Limit |
|---|---|
| Pro | 10,000 |
| Business | 20,000 |
| Scale | 50,000 |

- Response headers on every request:
  - `X-Monthly-RateLimit-Limit`: Your quota for the current month
  - `X-Monthly-RateLimit-Remaining`: Requests remaining this month
  - `X-Monthly-RateLimit-Reset`: Unix timestamp for the first of next month (UTC)
- An email warning is sent when usage reaches 80% of the monthly limit.
- Your quota can change during a month — Spiffy support can grant a temporary increase, which
  ends at the reset. `X-Monthly-RateLimit-Limit` always reflects the quota currently in force,
  so read it per response rather than caching the table above.

When either limit is exceeded, the API returns **429 Too Many Requests**. The two
limits return different error codes, and they need different handling — branch on
`error.code` rather than on the status alone.

Per-minute limit exceeded. Retryable; a `Retry-After` header gives the number of
seconds to wait:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "rate_limit_exceeded",
    "message": "Too many requests"
  }
}
```

Monthly quota exhausted. **Not retryable** — there is no `Retry-After` header, and
requests will continue to fail until the quota resets at the start of the next
month (see `X-Monthly-RateLimit-Reset`). Retrying will not succeed, and each
rejected attempt is itself counted, so a retry loop consumes the quota it is
waiting on:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "monthly_limit_exceeded",
    "message": "Monthly API request limit exceeded"
  }
}
```

## Pagination

List endpoints return paginated results to improve performance. You control pagination using query parameters:

| Parameter | Default | Maximum | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `page` | 1 | - | Page number (1-based) |
| `per_page` | 50 | 100 | Items per page |

**Example request:**
```
GET /v2/customers?page=2&per_page=25
```

**Response format:**
```json
{
  "data": [
    { "id": "cus_123", "email": "john@example.com", ... },
    { "id": "cus_124", "email": "jane@example.com", ... }
  ],
  "meta": {
    "pagination": {
      "page": 2,
      "page_size": 25,
      "total_count": 150,
      "total_pages": 6,
      "has_more": true
    }
  }
}
```

Note that `pagination` is nested inside `meta`, not at the top level.

The `meta.pagination` object provides:
- `page`: Current page number
- `page_size`: Items per page (same as the `per_page` parameter)
- `total_count`: Total number of items across all pages
- `total_pages`: Total number of pages
- `has_more`: Whether another page follows this one

`has_more` is the value to loop on. Paging until a request returns an empty
`data` array works, but costs one extra request per resource per run, and every
request counts against your quota.

Pagination is offset-based. There is no cursor, and no `next` link in the
envelope — advance by incrementing `page`.

## Filtering

Most list endpoints support filtering to narrow results. Filters use a dot notation syntax for operators:

| Syntax | Operator | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `?filter[field]=value` | Exact match | `?filter[status]=active` |
| `?filter[field.contains]=value` | Contains (case-insensitive) | `?filter[email.contains]=gmail` |
| `?filter[field.gt]=value` | Greater than | `?filter[amount.gt]=100` |
| `?filter[field.gte]=value` | Greater than or equal | `?filter[created_at.gte]=2025-01-01` |
| `?filter[field.lt]=value` | Less than | `?filter[amount.lt]=500` |
| `?filter[field.lte]=value` | Less than or equal | `?filter[updated_at.lte]=2025-12-31` |
| `?filter[field.in]=value1,value2` | In list | `?filter[status.in]=active,trialing` |
| `?filter[field.nin]=value1,value2` | Not in list | `?filter[status.nin]=canceled,expired` |

**Complex example:**
```
GET /v2/customers?filter[email.contains]=john&filter[created_at.gte]=2025-01-01&filter[status]=active
```

This finds active customers with "john" in their email address created after January 1st, 2025.

### Unrecognized parameters are ignored, not rejected

Filtering, expansion, search and sort all fail open. A filter key that is not
supported for a resource, an `include=` value that does not exist, `search=` on
an endpoint with no searchable fields, and `sort=` on a field that is not
sortable are each dropped silently. The request returns **200** with a normal
body — unfiltered, or unexpanded.

This is worth designing around, because nothing in the response tells you it
happened: a filter that looks reasonable but is not in the parameter list for
that specific endpoint will return your entire table, one page at a time, and
the code will look correct. Check the parameters documented for the exact
endpoint you are calling rather than assuming a field that exists on the object
is filterable.

Values are validated once a key is recognized — an unknown enum value returns
**400** listing the valid ones, and a malformed date or number returns **400**
naming the field.

## Searching

List endpoints support full-text search using the `search` parameter. Search is case-insensitive and works across multiple text fields relevant to each resource type.

**Example:**
```
GET /v2/customers?search=smith
```

This searches across customer names, emails, company names, and other text fields for the term "smith".

Search can be combined with filters and pagination:
```
GET /v2/customers?search=smith&filter[status]=active&page=2
```

## Resource Expansion

Many endpoints support expanding related resources in a single request using the `include` parameter. This reduces the number of API calls needed to fetch related data.

**Example:**
```
GET /v2/customers/cus_123?include=cards,stats,fields
```

This returns the customer with their payment cards, statistics, and custom fields included:

```json
{
  "id": "cus_123",
  "email": "john@example.com",
  "name": "John Smith",
  // ... other customer fields ...
  "cards": [
    { "id": "card_456", "last4": "4242", "brand": "Visa" }
  ],
  "stats": {
    "total_orders": 15,
    "total_spent": 1250.00,
    "avg_order_value": 83.33
  },
  "fields": [
    { "name": "preferred_contact", "value": "email" }
  ]
}
```

Available expansions are listed in each endpoint's documentation. Multiple expansions can be requested as a comma-separated list.

## Webhooks

Webhooks push changes to you instead of you polling for them, and deliveries do
not count against your API quota. Manage endpoints under
`/v2/webhook-endpoints`.

### Event types

`GET /v2/webhook-event-types` returns the live catalog and needs no
authentication. **Treat it as the source of truth** — subscribe from it rather
than from a hardcoded list.

The `events` array on an endpoint is not validated against the catalog. A
misspelled type is accepted, stored, and never fires, with no error at creation
time and nothing in the delivery log to inspect, because no delivery is ever
attempted. Omitting `events` subscribes to everything.

### Verifying the signature

Every delivery carries a `Spiffy-Signature` header:

```
Spiffy-Signature: t=1755043200,v1=3f8a...c4
```

- `t` is the Unix timestamp at signing.
- `v1` is a hex-encoded HMAC-SHA256, using your endpoint's signing secret as the
  key, over the exact string `{t}.{raw request body}`.

Sign the **raw body as received**. Parsing the JSON and re-serializing it will
change key order or spacing and the signature will not match.

```js
const crypto = require('crypto');

function verify(rawBody, header, secret) {
    const parts = Object.fromEntries(header.split(',').map(p => p.split('=')));
    const expected = crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret)
        .update(parts.t + '.' + rawBody)
        .digest('hex');
    return crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(expected), Buffer.from(parts.v1));
}
```

Compare with a constant-time function, and reject deliveries whose `t` is
outside a tolerance you choose, so an intercepted payload cannot be replayed
later. The signing secret is returned when you create an endpoint, and again
from `POST /v2/webhook-endpoints/{id}/rotate-secret`.

### Delivery

Delivery is **at-least-once and unordered**. The same event will eventually
arrive twice, and a later state change can arrive before an earlier one.
Deduplicate on the envelope `id`, and compare the object's own timestamps
before writing rather than assuming the newest delivery is the newest truth.

A delivery succeeds on any 2xx within 10 seconds. Respond first and do your work
afterward — once you return 2xx the event is considered delivered and will not
be sent again.

Failures retry 7 times over roughly 34 hours: immediately, then after 1 minute,
5 minutes, 30 minutes, 2 hours, 8 hours and 24 hours. An endpoint that
accumulates 50 consecutive failures is disabled automatically and its owners are
emailed; any success resets the counter.

Events are only queued for endpoints that were active when they fired, so
anything that happened while an endpoint was down, disabled or unsubscribed
cannot be backfilled. Pair webhooks with a low-frequency
`filter[updated_at.gte]` sweep to close that gap.

Endpoint URLs must be HTTPS and publicly resolvable; hostnames resolving to
private or loopback addresses are refused at delivery time.

## Not supported

These do not exist. They are listed so you can design around them rather than
discovering them in production:

- **Cursor pagination.** Offset/page only, as described above.
- **Sparse fieldsets.** `fields` is a reserved parameter name but is not
  implemented; responses always carry the full resource.
- **Idempotency keys.** No endpoint reads an `Idempotency-Key` header, so a
  retried `POST` is a second write. Deduplicate in your own application.
- **Conditional requests.** The API sets no `ETag`, `Last-Modified` or
  `Cache-Control` semantics, and no endpoint short-circuits on a request
  validator. A repeated identical `GET` is a full query and a full quota unit,
  so any caching has to be yours.
- **Bulk writes.** Every write is one resource per request. For bulk *reads*,
  use `filter[id.in]` with `per_page=100`, or a report export.

## Errors

The API uses standard HTTP status codes and returns detailed error information in a consistent JSON format:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "error_code",
    "message": "Human-readable error message",
    "details": {}  // Optional field-specific errors
  }
}
```

### Error Codes

| Status | Code | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 400 | `bad_request` | The request was invalid or malformed |
| 401 | `unauthorized` | Authentication is required or has failed |
| 403 | `forbidden` | You do not have permission to access this resource |
| 403 | `invalid_scope` | Missing required OAuth scope |
| 404 | `not_found` | The requested resource does not exist |
| 409 | `conflict` | The request conflicts with the current state (e.g., duplicate email) |
| 422 | `validation_error` | The request data failed validation |
| 429 | `rate_limit_exceeded` | Too many requests |
| 500 | `internal_error` | An unexpected server error occurred |

### Validation Errors

Validation errors include additional details about which fields failed:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "validation_error",
    "message": "Validation failed",
    "details": {
      "fieldErrors": {
        "email": ["Invalid email format"],
        "name": ["String must contain at least 1 character(s)"]
      }
    }
  }
}
```

post.summary: Create a report run (queued for background execution)
post.description:
Create a new report run. Returns 202 Accepted with the run in "pending" status.
Execution is asynchronous: a background worker picks up pending runs, so runs
typically START within about 30 seconds of creation, then take a few seconds to
a few minutes to finish depending on data volume.

Polling: call get_report_run until status is "completed" or "failed". Each poll
counts against the monthly API quota — poll no faster than every ~30 seconds
(matches the worker pickup cadence); typical runs complete within a couple of minutes.

Reading results: when completed, the run includes a stats block (flat_stats) that
